extracted.intended_audience: math-olympiad contestants and advanced problem-solvers (high-school / undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, named inequalities, and proof strategies for solving olympiad-style inequalities and related triangle/geometry inequalities. Includes examples, equality cases, and multiple proof methods for central results (AM-GM, Cauchy–Schwarz, rearrangement, Weitzenböck, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform into sum-of-squares form
rubrics_metrics.description: One strategy for proving inequalities is to transform them into the form x^2 ≥ 0 or Σ xi^2 ≥ 0 (i.e., reduce to nonnegativity of squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often a long road but is a fundamental approach; derive consequences equivalent to x^2 ≥ 0 or Σ xi^2 ≥ 0 and show equality cases when all squares vanish. Examples: reduce symmetric expressions to sums of squares as in proofs of (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) ≥ ab + bc + ca by writing as (a−b)^2+(b−c)^2+(c−a)^2 ≥ 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use homogeneity and normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit homogeneity of an inequality (f(ta, tb, tc) = t^k f(a,b,c)) to normalize variables (e.g., set a + b + c = 1 or scale so a = 1) to simplify the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization reduces number of parameters and often allows assuming extremal orderings (e.g., a ≥ b ≥ c). Use scaling to set convenient sums/products to 1 when f is homogeneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order variables / extremal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume an ordering among variables (e.g., a ≥ b ≥ c) for symmetric inequalities to simplify the argument and allow substitutions or bounding by extremal elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used in conjunction with homogeneity; replacing variables by extremal choices can reduce to proving nonnegativity of simpler expressions. Example: assume a ≥ b ≥ c in several proofs to get factorizations or comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze equality cases to guide proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture and use equality conditions (e.g., equality for equilateral triangle, or for all equal variables) to shape and check the chosen method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many proofs are designed so equality occurs exactly at the anticipated configuration (e.g., a = b = c for Weitzenböck). Use this to pick substitutions or factorings that vanish at equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM-GM and mean inequalities (HM-GM-AM-QM chain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arithmetic-geometric-harmonic-quadratic mean relations: min ≤ GM ≤ AM ≤ QM ≤ max and related inequalities to bound symmetric expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply AM-GM to products, use chained inequalities for quick bounds (e.g., a1···an ≤ ((a1+...+an)/n)^n), and employ mean inequalities for normalization and estimating sums of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from nonnegativity of quadratic polynomials; equality iff the vectors are linearly dependent. Used to prove AM-QM, to bound linear combinations (e.g., a sin x + b cos x ≤ √(a^2 + b^2)), and many symmetric inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement Inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences a1,...,an and b1,...,bn, the sum Σ ai ci (ci a permutation of b) is maximal when sequences are similarly sorted and minimal when they are oppositely sorted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by pairwise switching argument: swapping two entries changes sum by (ar−as)(cs−cr). Use the greedy matching idea in optimization examples; apply to matrix/sequence comparisons and to derive many other inequalities by permuting terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev Inequality for means
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by summing cyclic inequalities produced by rearrangement. For oppositely sorted sequences the reverse inequality holds. Useful to relate product-of-averages to average-of-products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scalar-product / vector viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret sums like Σ aibi as scalar products of vectors and apply vector inequalities (Cauchy–Schwarz, ordering) to deduce bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint clarifies equality conditions (linear dependence) and allows application of norm inequalities (e.g., ||a||·||b|| bounds). Useful for maximizing linear trigonometric forms and matrix inequality reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM-HM product form (Cauchy consequence)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be obtained from Cauchy–Schwarz or by combinatorial counting of 1's in product expansion; use to bound harmonic means and derive Nesbitt-like inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nesbitt's Inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive a,b,c: a/(b+c) + b/(a+c) + c/(a+b) ≥ 3/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple proofs: substitution x=b+c etc., AM-HM, AM-GM, or normalization; equality at a=b=c. Useful as a standard benchmark inequality; techniques shown (variable substitution to x,y,z and application of AM-HM and GM–AM) generalize to similar cyclic sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality forms and their use
rubrics_metrics.description: Four equivalent forms for triangle sides: (I) a+b>c etc.; (II) a>|b−c| etc.; (III) (a+b−c)(b+c−a)(c+a−b)>0; (IV) represent sides as sums x+y etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a triple are triangle sides; use appropriate form depending on whether you need sign positivity, absolute difference bounds, or substitution by half-sum variables x,y,z to simplify expressions in triangle-specific inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary symmetric functions for symmetric inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce u = a+b+c, v = ab+bc+ca, w = abc to rewrite symmetric polynomial inequalities compactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This often simplifies derivations (e.g., bisector inequality, or reductions in E10) and helps compare coefficients or factor expressions; useful for homogeneous symmetric inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weitzenböck's inequality for triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: For triangle sides a,b,c with area A: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 ≥ 4√3 A, with equality for the equilateral triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many proofs: geometric decompositions (deviations from equilateral), cosine law manipulations, Heron's formula + AM-GM, convexity (1/sin x convex), or Hadwiger–Finsler generalization. Use equality-case expectation to guide method choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hadwiger–Finsler inequality (generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stronger generalization related to triangle inequalities: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 ≥ (a−b)^2 + (b−c)^2 + (c−a)^2 + 4A·(tan(α/2)+tan(β/2)+tan(γ/2)), with convexity-based lower bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation uses trigonometric identities (1−cos α = 2 sin^2(α/2)) and convexity of tan on (0, π/2). Apply to get sharper bounds than Weitzenböck; equality at equilateral triangle where α=β=γ=60°.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use convexity / Jensen's inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use convexity of functions (e.g., f(x)=1/sin x, f(x)=tan x) and Jensen-type averaging (f(α)+f(β)+f(γ) ≥ 3 f((α+β+γ)/3)) to derive inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly effective in triangle angle-sum contexts: normalize α+β+γ=π and apply convexity to get lower/upper bounds; used in proofs 5 and 8 of Weitzenböck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitutions tailored to problem structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce substitutions that simplify structure (e.g., set a=y+z, b=z+x, c=x+y for triangle problems; set z=−x to eliminate cubes; use x=(b−a)b in Diophantine parameterizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitutions exploit symmetries or standard identities (e.g., bisector division, to convert side-length expressions into rational functions of x,y,z), often reducing problems to known inequalities or integer parameter recurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit factorization identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use classical algebraic factorizations such as a^3 + b^3 + c^3 − 3abc = (a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2−ab−bc−ca) to transform and compare expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factorizations reveal nonnegativity or allow application of AM-GM; e.g., combine with (a^2+b^2+c^2) ≥ ab+bc+ca to deduce lower bounds like a^3+b^3+c^3 ≥ 3abc (AM-GM for three numbers).
